```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

APCH asks, for each effect unit (a SNP or a gene), which subset of features
(traits or tissues) it affects jointly. It reports a subset only when every
feature in that subset is non-null, the partial conjunction hypothesis (PCH)
alternative. This vignette simulates a small data set and runs the full
analysis on two cores.

```{r library}
library(apch)
```

## Simulated data

We simulate 10,000 effects on four traits. Most effects are null, some affect
one trait, and the rest affect several traits at once. Jointly active effects
share one magnitude state (small or large) across their traits, which is the
kind of sharing APCH-s learns. Estimation errors are correlated across traits
with correlation 0.3, as happens with overlapping GWAS samples.

```{r simulate}
simulate_apch_example <- function(n, p = 4, rho = 0.3, seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  configs <- as.matrix(expand.grid(rep(list(0:1), p)))
  size <- rowSums(configs)
  prob <- ifelse(size == 0, 0.85,
          ifelse(size == 1, 0.08 / p,
          ifelse(size == p, 0.03, 0.04 / sum(size > 1 & size < p))))
  gamma <- configs[sample.int(nrow(configs), n, replace = TRUE, prob = prob), , drop = FALSE]
  scale <- sample(c(1, 3), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.7, 0.3))
  B <- gamma * matrix(rnorm(n * p, sd = rep(scale, p)), n, p)
  C <- matrix(rho, p, p); diag(C) <- 1
  Bhat <- B + matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p) %*% chol(C)
  colnames(Bhat) <- colnames(B) <- paste0("trait", seq_len(p))
  list(Bhat = Bhat, S = matrix(1, n, p), C = C, B = B)
}

dat <- simulate_apch_example(n = 10000)
dim(dat$Bhat)
```

`Bhat` holds the effect estimates and `S` their standard errors. Here we work
on the z-score scale, so `S` is all ones. `C` is the correlation of the
estimation errors across features. It can be a single matrix shared by all
effects, as here, or a list with one matrix per effect.

## Fitting APCH

```{r fit}
fit <- apch(
  Bhat = dat$Bhat, S = dat$S, C = dat$C,
  effect_id = paste0("snp", seq_len(nrow(dat$Bhat))),
  alpha = 0.05, workers = 2, verbose = FALSE
)
fit
```

By default `apch()` fits APCH-s, the model used in the paper: it learns how
effect sizes are shared among jointly affected features and prunes
unsupported allocation states before the final fit. Subsets are selected by
the subset-level local false sign rate (lfsr), which we recommend as the
primary criterion.

## Reading the calls

Each row of `fit$calls` is one effect together with the largest subset of
features declared jointly significant. `L` is the subset size.

```{r calls}
head(fit$calls)
table(L = fit$calls$L)
```

## Working with the fitted model

`apch()` runs the stages `apch_marginal()`, `apch_joint()` and
`apch_select()` in one call. The fitted object can be reused without
refitting. `apch_select()` selects at another level or with the lfdr, and
`apch_lfdr()` and `apch_lfsr()` return the subset-level quantities for any
subsets, given as rows of a 0/1 matrix.

```{r stages}
lfdr_calls <- apch_select(fit, alpha = 0.05, method = "lfdr")
nrow(lfdr_calls)

U <- rbind(all4 = c(1, 1, 1, 1), first2 = c(1, 1, 0, 0))
head(apch_lfsr(fit, subset = U, workers = 2))
```

## Checking the calls against the truth

A reported subset is a false discovery if any of its features is truly null.
Because we simulated the data, we can compute the false discovery proportion
directly and compare it with the target level of 0.05.

```{r fdp}
fdp <- function(calls, B) {
  idx <- match(calls$effect, paste0("snp", seq_len(nrow(B))))
  feats <- strsplit(calls$subset, "|", fixed = TRUE)
  false <- vapply(seq_along(idx), function(i) any(B[idx[i], feats[[i]]] == 0), logical(1))
  mean(false)
}
c(lfsr = fdp(fit$calls, dat$B), lfdr = fdp(lfdr_calls, dat$B))
```
